fluff.overview: The Jihad pushed the Capellan Confederation into a vicious cycle of attrition. Horrific equipment losses forced the House to field whatever weapons it could produce, from advanced stealth-armored BattleMeks to expendable Hetzer assault guns. Increasing reliance on inferior equipment drove casualty rates higher, which deepened a crippling manpower shortage. Trainees were rushed through abbreviated courses only to be killed in combat, forcing academies to push yet another ill-prepared class into the field. Mujika Aerospace approached the Strategios with a solution to both problems: the Bullet Suicide Drone, a remotely piloted expendable fighter that could put inexperienced operators into real combat without risking their lives.
fluff.capabilities:
The Bullet is, by design, an inferior version of the already-spartan Guardian conventional fighter. Its engine and missile system are smaller, and it lacks VSTOL capability, requiring prepared runways for operation. The sole external improvement is a modest increase in armor over the Guardian baseline. What makes the Bullet tactically significant is the absence of a cockpit and pilot compartment entirely.

Taking a page from Word of Blake drone warfare, Mujika installed a remote operating system that allows a pilot to control the fighter from a distance far enough that targeting the operator is impractical during active combat. The Bullet's nose-mounted SRM 2 provides token offensive capability, but its primary weapon is a powerful internal explosive charge. Designed to look and behave like a damaged Guardian, the Bullet is routinely ignored by anti-aircraft defenders focused on more dangerous aerospace fighters--until the moment it slams into a command center or DropShip in a devastating kamikaze strike.
fluff.deployment: Capellan militias began purchasing Bullets by the dozen, deploying them en masse the moment any hostile force entered the atmosphere. The Word of Blake was caught completely off guard when entire squadrons of what appeared to be manned Guardian fighters unwaveringly slammed into their transports and landing zones, destroying assets worth far more than the drones themselves while the operators remained safely distant. Even AFFS forces were caught out--on New Hessen, two dozen Bullets acquired through shell mercenary companies destroyed two Word of Blake supply transports before the Blakists secured their landing zone.
fluff.history:
The Bullet's introduction during the Jihad created an immediate tactical dilemma for opposing forces. After the New Hessen operation demonstrated that the drones could appear in unexpected theaters, Word of Blake commanders began diverting fire from legitimate aerospace fighters to engage any conventional fighter that might be an explosive drone attempting to close with high-value targets. In the vast majority of cases, these were manned aircraft, not Bullets.

The consequences were severe and far-reaching. Conventional fighter pilots facing Word of Blake attackers saw their casualty rates increase tenfold as Blakist gunners reflexively targeted them first, assuming any conventional airframe might be a suicide drone. The Bullet thus achieved an effect far beyond its direct combat impact: by forcing the enemy to treat every cheap atmospheric fighter as a potential guided missile, it degraded the effectiveness of Blakist air defense doctrine and provided indirect protection to the Confederation's more valuable aerospace assets. Mujika continued production at St. Ives throughout the Jihad and into the post-war period, as the drone's low cost and proven effectiveness ensured steady demand from Capellan garrison commands.
